messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi remembers the night it ended not as a single event, but as a series of sensory fragments that refuse to stay in the past. It began with the look in his ex-partner’s eyes—a possessive, appraising stare that made Kofi feel less like a person and more like an object to be controlled. The argument that followed is a blur, but he can still hear his partner’s voice, a low, menacing whisper repeating the same phrase over and over, an auditory loop that plays in his head without warning. He remembers the sharp, metallic taste of blood filling his mouth after his lip split against the floor. And he remembers the sterile, chemical smell of the emergency room where he spent the next six hours, a scent that now seems to cling to every corner of his life. That was nine months ago.

In the time since, the world has become a landscape of potential threats. As a parole officer, Kofi’s job requires him to sit in small, enclosed rooms with men, many of whom have a history of violence. He used to pride himself on his ability to connect, to be firm but fair. Now, every client interview is an exercise in terror. He finds himself unable to meet their eyes, his gaze fixed on a spot on the wall just over their shoulder. He feels his body lock up, his shoulders bunching around his ears, a posture of constant readiness for an attack that never comes. He watches their hands, their shifting weight, the subtle changes in their expression, certain that he is moments away from having to defend himself. He knows, logically, that he is safe, but the feeling of being alone with a man in a closed space is suffocating. He has started letting minor infractions slide, avoiding the necessary confrontations of his job simply because the thought of any disagreement, however small, sends a jolt of panic through him. His supervisor recently noted his "decreased engagement" in his performance review.

The memories are not like memories at all; they feel like visitations. Last week, a janitor used an antiseptic cleaner on a countertop in the office breakroom. The smell hit Kofi instantly, and he was no longer in his workplace. He was back on the cold floor of his old apartment, the taste of blood sharp on his tongue, his ex-partner’s whispered words echoing in his ears as if he were standing right beside him. The memory was so vivid, so present, that he flinched, dropping his coffee mug, which shattered on the tile. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, until a colleague asked if he was alright. He couldn't explain that for a full thirty seconds, he had not been there at all.

This pervasive sense of threat has poisoned every part of his life. He is in a new relationship with a kind, patient woman, but he finds himself pushing her away. When she shows him affection or when a moment of genuine happiness begins to surface, a cold dread washes over him. Joy feels like a trap, a dangerous vulnerability he cannot afford. He has come to believe that his life was irrevocably broken that night. The injustice of it is a constant, bitter pill; his ex-partner faced no consequences, while Kofi feels he is serving a life sentence. He sees his career faltering, his new relationship strained by a distance he creates but cannot seem to dismantle. He feels hollowed out. It was this creeping, persistent thought—that perhaps his life was no longer worth the exhausting effort of living it—that finally propelled him to seek help. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate fear that the man he was before the trauma is gone for good.
